newsitem.title: USA: American Airlines faces threat of February strike.
newsitem.headline: American Airlines faces threat of February strike.

text.p: American Airlines and its pilots turned down binding arbitration in their bitter contract dispute on Wednesday and entered a 30-day "cooling off" period that could lead to a strike or a lockout on Feb. 15.
The moves came the same day that American's Fort Worth, Texas-based parent company AMR Corp. announced that 1996 was its most profitable year ever.

Airline management had insisted the pilots union accept binding arbitration by Wednesday morning. When pilots ignored the deadline, the airline itself declined the arbitration offer and the cooling off period was immediately triggered.

Under federal law, both sides can try to thrash out an accord in the next 30 days but, if they fail, the union will be free to stage a walk-out starting Feb. 15 while the carrier could implement new work conditions or lock out its pilots.
As both sides jockeyed for a strong negotiating position, company executives said they feared the pilots' demands were threatening the very future of the country's second largest carrier.

"We quite frankly are at a loss as to what to do next; accept a contract that would be at best uncompetitive vs. our principal competitors, or a possible cessation of operations. Two disastrous sort of alternatives," Chief Financial Officer Gerard Arpey told reporters.

He said the pilots' wage and conditions demands would cripple the airline's ability to compete and scuttle its plans for modest growth, including a $6.5 billion order for 103 jets from Boeing Co. which was announced in November but which has now been put on ice.
While American was embroiled in the labour dispute, its parent AMR Corp. reported record profits for 1996.
AMR ran up an operating profit of $854 million, or $9.77 per share, for 1996. When special one-time items were included, the year's profit rose to $1.02 billion, or $11.19 per share.
In the last three months of 1996, the airline earned $284 million, or $3.08 a share, compared with a loss of $282 million, or $3.69 a share, in the same period of 1995.
Pilots immediately jumped on the figures to push their case that they had taken a hit when the airline industry was in the doldrums and now deserved a share of the spoils.

Rank-and-file members of the Allied Pilots Association last week rejected a tentative four-year labour contract which union leaders had agreed to last September, and have since drawn up a list of frsh demands.

They include pay raises of more than 11 percent over the next four years, options on 7.25 million company shares at a discount of $10 each, and a guarantee that American would not use its commuter carrier to fly 50-passenger regional jets.

"Our proposal is a bottom-line minimum," union spokesman Wally Pitts said on Wednesday. "It is certainly not going to bankrupt the company. Our wage requests are reasonable, all we want is a cost of living increase."

Pitts said the union's new demands would represent additional costs of $200 million over the life of a four-year contract, while the carrier would lose $300 million in advanced bookings over the next 30 days, and much more in the event of a strike.
Both sides stepped up their rhetorical attacks, while also insisting that they still want to avoid a strike.

"We stress that the airline remains hopeful that we will reach an amicable resolution with our pilots and that a strike can be avoided given that our position on pay and other issues is very fair," American said in a hotline message.
Pitts said the ball was in management's court.
"We are not seeking conflict but if they force us into a strike, we are ready for it. Our membership has overwhelmingly shown it is ready to strike."
Both sides admitted they are far apart on the issues.
Although it was rejected by pilots, the tentative agreement reached in September had also failed to please AMR executives and now they are being pushed for more concessions.

"We weren't giving each other high-fives because of the deal we did and now we face the prospect of something even worse, or a confrontation," Arpey said. "So there really aren't any very good options for the company right now."
AMR shares rose $2.25 on the New York Stock Exchange after its results were released but then dropped back amid concerns about a possible strike and ended the day unchanged at $83.50.
